title: The history of the hot air balloon
tagline: From a legend of lanterns to a flight round the world, in about 240 years of ballooning.
intro: In June 1783 two brothers in a French town lit a fire under a huge paper-lined bag and watched it rise. Within six months people were flying in it. Ever since, balloons have chased height, distance and the wind.

eras.name: Lanterns and legends
eras.summary: Small lanterns lifted by fire, a few early experiments, and a gas that nobody yet knew how to use.

eras.name: The first balloons
eras.summary: Within months in 1783, a hot air balloon and a hydrogen balloon carried people into the sky.

eras.name: Gas, war and spectacle
eras.summary: Gas balloons crossed countries, carried mail out of a besieged city, and climbed higher than anyone could breathe.

eras.name: Edge of space
eras.summary: Sealed gondolas took people into the stratosphere, and some paid with their lives.

eras.name: The propane age
eras.summary: Nylon and propane made hot air ballooning a sport. Balloons also crossed oceans and circled the globe.

events.title: The Kongming lantern, a legend
events.text: Tradition says the general Zhuge Liang used a sky lantern to send for help when enemy troops surrounded him, so the lanterns carry his name. The article we checked cites no source from his own time. Treat it as a legend, not a record.
events.why: It shows how old the idea of a small lantern lifted by hot air may be.

events.title: A small balloon in Lisbon
events.text: Accounts say Gusmão showed the court a small balloon lifted by the heat of a flame. His large “passarola” airship was never flown in public. A later London report gives a different year, 1720, so the evidence is thin.
events.why: It is among the earliest reported hot air balloon demonstrations, but it is poorly documented.

events.title: Cavendish describes “inflammable air”
events.text: Cavendish told the Royal Society about a light gas he made by dissolving metals in acids. He called it “inflammable air”. We now call it hydrogen.
events.why: A gas far lighter than air would soon lift the first gas balloons.

events.title: The Montgolfier balloon rises over Annonay
events.text: The brothers launched an unmanned cloth-and-paper balloon about 10.5 m wide, heated by a straw fire. It rose roughly 1,000 m, stayed up about 10 minutes and came down more than 2 km away.
events.why: This public launch began the age of flight.

events.title: The first hydrogen balloon
events.who: Jacques Charles and the Robert brothers
events.text: An unmanned hydrogen balloon of about 35 cubic metres rose from Paris and drifted north. After about 45 minutes it came down near Gonesse, roughly 15 to 21 km away, where frightened villagers wrecked it.
events.why: It showed that a light gas could lift a balloon, and began a rival to hot air.

events.title: A sheep, a duck and a rooster at Versailles
events.text: A sheep, a duck and a rooster rose in a Montgolfier balloon. They floated about 8 minutes and landed safely, about 3 km away.
events.why: It showed that living things could survive the trip before any person went up.

events.title: The first people fly free
events.who: Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d’Arlandes
events.text: Two men flew across Paris in a Montgolfier hot air balloon. The flight took about 25 minutes and covered about 9 km. One account gives a top height of about 900 m.
events.why: People left the ground in free flight for the first time.

events.title: Charles and Robert fly a hydrogen balloon
events.text: Their hydrogen balloon flew about 2 hours and about 36 km, to roughly 550 m, and had a valve and sand ballast. Robert then stepped out and Charles rose alone, higher than a mile.
events.why: It set the plan for the gas balloon that lasted for generations.

events.title: Élisabeth Thible flies at Lyon
events.text: With a man named Fleurant, Thible flew about 45 minutes and about 4 km in the hot air balloon La Gustave. She is described as the first woman on record to fly in an untethered hot air balloon.
events.why: Women were in the air within a year of the first flight.

events.title: The first balloon flight in England
events.text: Lunardi rose with a dog, a cat and a pigeon. He touched down briefly at North Mymms to put the unwell cat out, then landed at Standon Green End in Hertfordshire.
events.why: Ballooning reached Britain as a public spectacle.

events.title: Across the English Channel
events.text: Blanchard and the American doctor John Jeffries took off from Dover and became the first to cross the Channel by air.
events.why: The first crossing of the sea by air.

events.title: The first aviation disaster
events.who: Pilâtre de Rozier and Pierre-Jules Romain
events.text: Their balloon, which paired a hydrogen envelope with a small hot air one, caught fire about 30 minutes after launch from Boulogne. Both men died. A modern study points to a static spark, not the flame.
events.why: It showed the danger of putting a flame near hydrogen.

events.title: The first balloon flight in North America
events.text: Blanchard rose from a prison yard in Philadelphia and landed in Gloucester County, New Jersey.
events.why: Ballooning crossed the Atlantic as a show.

events.title: Sophie Blanchard dies in Paris
events.text: Blanchard was widely described as the first woman to work as a professional balloonist, and Napoleon is said to have named her Aeronaut of the Official Festivals. During a fireworks show at Tivoli a rocket set her balloon alight. It came down over rooftops and she was thrown out and killed.
events.why: Women were star aeronauts, and the risks were real.

events.title: London to Germany in one night
events.who: Charles Green, Robert Holland and Thomas Monck-Mason
events.text: In a gas balloon they flew about 608 km in 18 hours.
events.why: It was the first crewed gas balloon flight over 600 km.

events.title: Too high to breathe
events.text: Glaisher passed out at about 8,800 m. Coxwell, with numb hands, managed to free the valve so they could descend. Later estimates of their top height run from over 9,500 m to 10,900 m.
events.why: It tested what a human body could take in thin air.

events.title: Mail flies out of besieged Paris
events.text: During the Siege of Paris the balloon Neptune flew the first mail out on 23 September. Around 66 balloon flights left the city. Five were captured and three went missing. Léon Gambetta flew out on 7 October.
events.why: Balloons became the first large air mail and escape route.

events.title: Berson and Süring reach about 10,800 m
events.text: In the balloon Preussen they rose to about 10,800 m for a scientific flight.
events.why: Scientific flights opened up the upper air.

events.title: Into the stratosphere
events.text: In a sealed, pressurised gondola under a hydrogen balloon they reached 15,781 m, the first people in the stratosphere. They launched at Augsburg and landed near Gurgl, Austria. Some sources give Kipfer’s first name as Charles.
events.why: A pressurised cabin made flight above the weather possible.

events.title: The Osoaviakhim-1 disaster
events.who: Pavel Fedoseenko, Andrey Vasenko and Ilya Usyskin
events.text: The hydrogen balloon reached about 22,000 m. It lost lift on the way down and fell, killing all three crew.
events.why: It showed the price of record chasing.

events.title: Explorer II sets a record
events.who: Albert W. Stevens and Orvil A. Anderson
events.text: Their helium balloon reached 22,066 m and landed safely near White Lake, South Dakota. The record stood for nearly two decades.
events.why: It was a long-lived altitude record.

events.title: Ed Yost flies the first modern hot air balloon
events.text: Yost flew a hot air balloon with its own burner on board, the first free flight of the modern kind. Sources differ on how long it lasted, from 25 minutes to 1 hour 35 minutes.
events.why: It began the modern sport of hot air ballooning.

events.title: Strato-Lab V reaches 34,668 m
events.text: They reached 113,740 feet (34.67 km) in about 10 hours. Prather drowned during the helicopter transfer after landing.
events.why: It is listed as the highest balloon flight on record.

events.title: A hot air balloon crosses the Channel
events.text: The British Balloon Museum dates this first hot air balloon Channel crossing to 25 March. Wikipedia gives 13 April.
events.why: Hot air ballooning showed it could cross water.

events.title: The first Albuquerque Balloon Fiesta
events.who: Local balloonists and radio station KOB
events.text: Thirteen balloons gathered in a shopping-centre car park for the radio station’s 50th birthday. By 2000 the fiesta had 1,019 registered balloons.
events.why: It became one of the world’s largest balloon events.

events.title: Double Eagle II crosses the Atlantic
events.who: Ben Abruzzo, Maxie Anderson and Larry Newman
events.where: Presque Isle, Maine, to Miserey, France
events.text: They flew for 137 hours 6 minutes and about 3,100 miles (about 4,990 km), and landed in a wheat field near Miserey, northwest of Paris.
events.why: It was the first balloon crossing of the Atlantic.

events.title: Across the Pacific in a hot air balloon
events.text: The FAI lists a hot air balloon distance record of 7,671.91 km, from Miyakonojo in Japan to Yellowknife in Canada, with Lindstrand as pilot and Branson as crew.
events.why: It was the first Pacific crossing by hot air balloon.

events.title: Around the world without stopping
events.text: Breitling Orbiter 3 flew for 19 days 21 hours 55 minutes, from the Swiss Alps to the Egyptian desert. Its track was about 40,800 km. Sources date the landing 20 or 21 March.
events.why: The first nonstop balloon flight around the world.

events.title: Fossett flies round the world alone
events.text: Fossett covered about 33,195 km in his balloon Spirit of Freedom, with about 13 days 8 hours of flight time.
events.why: The first solo balloon flight around the world.

events.title: India’s hot air balloon height record
events.text: Singhania reached 21,027 m in a Cameron Z-1600 hot air balloon. The FAI still lists it as the current record.
events.why: It is the hot air balloon altitude record.

people.name: Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier
people.note: They flew the first hot air balloon in public in 1783.

people.name: Jacques Charles
people.note: He flew the first crewed hydrogen balloon, with a valve and ballast.

people.name: Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier
people.note: He made the first free flight and died in the first aviation disaster.

people.name: Élisabeth Thible
people.note: She flew in a hot air balloon in 1784, the first woman on record to do so untethered.

people.name: Sophie Blanchard
people.note: She is widely described as the first woman to work as a professional balloonist.

people.name: Zhuge Liang
people.role: Strategist, linked by legend to the sky lantern
people.note: The story that he used lanterns to signal is a legend with no dated source.

people.name: Auguste Piccard
people.note: He took people into the stratosphere in a sealed gondola in 1931.

people.name: Ed Yost
people.note: He flew the first modern hot air balloon in 1960.

people.name: Vijaypat Singhania
people.note: He took a hot air balloon to 21,027 m in 2005.

people.name: Per Lindstrand
people.note: He piloted the 1991 hot air balloon crossing of the Pacific with Richard Branson.

series.title: How high people have flown in a balloon
series.caption: From a few hundred metres over Paris to the edge of space, in under 180 years.

points.label: Glaisher blacks out at about 8,800 m

series.title: How far a balloon has flown in one trip
series.caption: Round-the-world flights are left out, because they are track distances, not straight lines.

facts: The first Montgolfier balloon seen by the public, in 1783, carried nobody. It rose about 1,000 m.
The first passengers on the Versailles flight in 1783 were a sheep, a duck and a rooster.
The 1783 hydrogen balloon of Charles and Robert already had a valve and sand ballast.
Pilâtre de Rozier’s 1785 Channel balloon combined a hydrogen bag with a hot air bag.
Steve Fossett’s solo flight round the world in 2002 covered about 33,195 km.
